**Biomass-based Acidic Deep Eutectic Solvents for Efficient Dissolution of Lignin: Towards Performance and Mechanism Elucidation** Huixian Han 5',†, Lan Chen 5',†, Jiancheng Zhao 6',7', Haitao Yu 5', Yang Wang 5', Helian Yan 5', Yingxiong Wang 8', Zhimin Xue 5',*, Tiancheng Mu 9',* 5' Beijing Key Laboratory of Lignocellulosic Chemistry, Beijing Forestry University, Beijing 100083, China. 6' Shanxi Engineering Research Center of Biorefinery, Institute of Coal Chemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Taiyuan 030001, China. 7' Center of Materials Science and Optoelectronics Engineering, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100049, China. 8' College of Chemistry, Taiyuan University of Technology, Taiyuan 030024, China. 9' Department of Chemistry, Renmin University of China, Beijing 100872, China.

Abstract: Lignocellulose utilization has the unique feature of net-zero carbon emissions. Thus, the utilization of lignocellulose as a renewable alternative to fossil-based carbon resources is one of the most promising strategies to achieve "carbon neutrality". Lignin has been recognized as the most abundant aromatic biopolymer on Earth; hence, it could be the most promising alternative to fossil-based aromatics. The efficient dissolution of lignin is crucial for lignin upgrading, which relies on the design of innovative and robust solvents. Herein, we designed several biomass-derived acidic deep eutectic solvents (DESs) using choline chloride, betaine, and L-carnitine as hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs), and four protic compounds as <::transcription of the content : AL DAL EHL KL DES Lignin 80°C Lignin-DES solution AL Solubility (%) ChCl-based Bet-based L-carn-based DES Solubility (%) pKa 5.04 4.19 1.23 2 1.5 1.0 0.5 0.0 EO-based EA-based OA-based DES : figure::> hydrogen bond donors (HBDs), namely, oxalic acid, benzoic acid, ethyl gallate, and 5-methoxysalicylic acid. The designed DESs can dissolve different types of lignin, including alkali lignin (AL), dealkaline lignin (DAL), enzymatic hydrolysis lignin (EHL), and Kraft lignin (KL). Lignin dissolution was found to be affected by the relative contents of three phenylpropanoid monomers in lignin: syringyl (S), guaiacyl (G), and p-hydroxyphenyl (H) units. More S and fewer H units in lignin could result in higher solubility. G-, S-, and H-type structural units were found in EHL, while AL, KL, and DAL had only G-type structural units. Therefore, EHL could be more easily dissolved than AL, KL, and DAL in the most developed DESs. The hydroxyl group content of the four lignin samples had a significant impact on lignin dissolution. AL (1.98 mmol·g⁻¹) and EHL (1.93 mmol·g⁻¹) had much higher contents of phenolic hydroxyl groups than DAL (0.62 mmol·g⁻¹), implying that AL and EHL had higher polarity than DAL. This resulted in different dissolution behaviors in different DESs with varying polarities. However, the sulfonate groups afforded KL with much higher polarity, thus resulting in the special dissolution behavior of KL. It is to be noted that not all cases of dissolving lignin in the developed DESs conformed to the above rules. Therefore, it is necessary to further explore the effect of the properties of the DESs on the dissolution of different lignins. Choline chloride was the preferred HBA to construct DESs with good performance and adaptability to lignin dissolution, whereas suitable acidity enabled benzoic acid and ethyl gallate to be favorable HBDs. Systematic investigation revealed that an efficient DES for lignin dissolution should possess stronger hydrogen-bonding acidity (α > 0.95) and appropriate polarity matching with the dissolved lignin. In addition, the pKa value of the HBD and the acidity of the DESs were also efficient indices for estimating the performance of an acidic DES in dissolving lignin, and the pKa value and acidity could be well correlated with the polarity. Generally, HBDs (e.g., BA and EG in this study) with moderate pKa values can be employed to construct robust DESs to dissolve lignin with satisfactory solubility. # 1 Introduction Utilization of lignocellulose as a renewable alternative of fossil-based carbon resources (i.e., coal, oil, and natural gas) is one of the most promising strategies to achieve "carbon neutrality" considering that lignocellulose utilization has the unique feature of net-zero carbon emission ¹,². In this context, utilization of renewable and abundant-available biomass has gained worldwide interest ³,⁴. As one of the three main components of lignocellulose, lignin has been recognized as the most abundant aromatic biopolymer on earth, thereby affording lignin being the most promising alternative to fossil-based aromatics (i.e., chemicals and materials) ⁵⁻⁷. Especially, the concept of "lignin-first biorefinery" significantly promotes the development of lignin upgrading to produce useful chemicals and functional materials ⁸⁻¹⁰. Generally, dissolution of lignin in an appropriate solvent is unavoidable to realize the goal of effectively utilizing lignin. However, the complex cross-linked three-dimensional structure greatly hinders lignin dissolution ¹¹. To solve this challenging issue relays on designing robust and innovative solvent systems ¹²,¹³.

To date, various solvent systems have been developed to dissolve lignin, including aqueous organic solvents 14-17, liquid ammonia 18,19, ionic liquid (IL)-based systems 20-22, and deep eutectic solvents (DESs) 23-25. Of these developed solvents, DESs are an emerging class of functional solvents, and are generally composed by two components, calling as hydrogen-bond donor (HBD) and hydrogen-bond acceptor (HBA), respectively 26-28. In comparison with other solvent systems for lignin dissolution, DESs have some unique features. For example, DESs have lower volatility than organic solvents. Moreover, the process to prepare DESs is much simpler than that of synthesizing ILs, and organic solvents can be completely avoided for constructing DESs 27,29. More importantly, the components in DESs can accept (for HBAs) or donate (for HBDs) hydrogen bonding, endowing DESs the ability to form hydrogen bonding with lignin, which is indispensable for dissolving lignin in a solvent 11,30. These features make DESs be a highly promising class of solvents to dissolve lignin, and some DESs with good ability to dissolve lignin have been successfully developed. Generally, the DESs using protic chemicals (i.e.,

alcohols, carboxylic acids, amides, and phenols) as the HBDs showed stronger capability on dissolution of lignin 31-33. However, the properties of lignin varied with the resources of raw lignocellulose and the extraction strategies to obtain lignin, thereby resulting in the unsatisfactory adaptability of the developed DESs on different types of lignin. Additionally, most of the developed DESs often involved fossil-based chemicals. Utilization of biomass-based derivatives to prepare DESs is a highly attractive strategy to achieve a "closed-loop" biorefinery. Recent works revealed that DESs could be directly prepared using biomass-derived chemicals, affording these DESs being biocompatibility and biodegradability. This feature of biomass-derived DESs enabled one-pot biomass processing with good environmental friendliness and cost effectiveness 34-37. Although biomass-derived DESs have been prepared using choline chloride as the HBA and lactic acid or some lignin monomers as the HBDs for lignin dissolution or biomass pretreatment, the DESs prepared completely from renewable resources are still limited, and their capability of dissolving lignin needs to be further improved 23,38,39. In spite of the encouraging achievements of using DESs to dissolve lignin, innovative and robust DESs completely derived from renewable resources are still highly desirable with the goal of making the dissolution processes green to the greatest extent. In another aspect, how to select HBAs and HBDs to construct robust DESs with high solubility of lignin is also an urgent issue to be solved. To date, there still lack reasonable methods or suitable standard to accurately evaluate the capability of one DES on lignin dissolution, resulting in that much time was wasted to select efficient DESs to dissolve lignin. Therefore, exploring a general rule for evaluation of DES's dissolution capability remains a great challenge.

With the purpose of developing robust renewable DESs to dissolve lignin and establish a reasonable index to evaluate the ability of acidic DESs to dissolve lignin, herein, we constructed several renewable acidic DESs using biomass-based HBAs and HBDs. In these designed DESs, choline chloride (ChCl), betaine (Bet), and L-carnitine (L-Carn) were selected as the renewable HBAs, while four biomass-based protic compounds (i.e., oxalic acid (OA), benzoic acid (BA), ethyl gallate (EG), and 5-methoxysalicylic acid (5-MeOSA)) were employed as the HBDs. Four different types of lignin, including alkali lignin (AL), dealkaline lignin (DAL), Kraft lignin (KL), and enzymatic hydrolysis lignin (EHL), were selected to investigate the dissolution ability of the developed DESs. In these four types of lignin, AL was mainly derived from alkaline pulping black liquor and had a complex lignin condensation structure linked by C–C and ether bonds, while DAL was achieved from the residue obtained by alkali treatment of lignocellulose and subsequent acidizing separation. KL was usually produced by the reaction between lignin and lye when lignocellulose was cooked by the kraft method. The hydroxyl ions, sulfur ions and sulfhydryl ions in the kraft cooking liquor would effectively

promote de-methoxide of lignin to obtain KL with more phenolic hydroxyl groups. EHL was extracted from the enzymatic residue of lignocellulose, which preserved the original structures (phenolic hydroxyl groups, and ether bonds) of the lignin. It was observed that the obtained DESs could dissolve various types of lignin. Notably, all the DESs using ChCl as the HBA possessed good performance on dissolving lignin, while BA and EG were preferred HBDs to generate robust DESs owing to their suitable acidity (based on the pKa and the δP of trimethylphosphine oxide in 31P NMR spectra). These results represented the major finding of this work, which was beneficial for designing robust renewable DESs to dissolve lignin.

## 3 Results and discussion ### 3.1 Preparation and characterization of DESs The desired DESs in this work were constructed by heating the mixture of the HBAs and HBDs with a suitable molar ratio, and the detail route was described in the experimental section. DSC experiments indicated that the melting points of all the prepared DESs were below 100 °C (Table S1, and Figs. 1a and S1), which were much lower than the corresponding pure components. For instance, the melting points of L-Carn:5-MeOSA(1:1) and L-Carn:BA(1:1) were -16.85 °C and -27.55 °C, respectively, while the melting points of all the corresponding parent components were about 120 °C (Fig. 1a), confirming the formation of DESs from the selected HBAs and HBDs. The intermolecular hydrogen-bond interactions between HBAs and HBDs were investigated by FT-IR spectra (Figs. 1b and S2) 43. It can be noted that the absorption peaks of O—H stretching vibration at 3300 cm⁻¹ in EG changed to broader bands in the spectra of corresponding DESs, indicating the formation of highly associated hydrogen bonds in the prepared DESs. Besides, the thermal stability of acidic DESs were determined by TGA experiments 44. The initial decomposition temperatures of almost all the prepared DESs were about 120 °C (Fig. 1c), which suggested that the DESs were stable under the conditions of dissolving lignin. ## 3.2 Dissolution of AL in the prepared DESs The ability of the prepared DESs to dissolve lignin was initially evaluated using the dissolution of AL as the model at 80 °C (Table 1). As shown in Table 1, all the synthesized ChCl-based DESs showed good ability to dissolve AL (Table 1, entries 1–4), and the difference on AL solubility (41.5%–43.5%, mass fraction hereafter) was negligible when the type of HBD or the ChCl/HBD molar ratio changed. When the HBA was changed into Bet (Table 1, entries 5–7), the highest solubility of AL was only 26.0% using Bet:5-MeOSA(2:1) as the solvent (Table 1, entry 6). In comparison, the ability of L-Carn-based DESs (Table 1, entries 8–12) to dissolve AL was better than that of Bet-based DESs, and the highest AL solubility in L-Carn-based DESs could reach up to 36.3% using L-Carn:5-MeOSA(1:2) as the solvent (Table 1, entry 12). Additionally, the effect of HBAs on AL solubility could be intuitively observed when DESs were generated using the three HBAs with BA at a molar ratio of 1:2 (Table 1, entries 3, 5, and 9), and the AL solubility decreased as follows: ChCl:BA(1:2) (43.5%) > Bet:BA(1:2) (37.1%) > L-Carn:BA(1:2) (34.1%). These results confirmed the advantage of ChCl to form DESs with the good ability to dissolve AL.

Notably, for the DESs prepared using L-Carn and ChCl as the HBA, the AL solubility increased with the decreased HBA/HBD molar ratio, in other words, with the increase of HBD proportion, because more HBD had more sites to generate hydrogen bonding with AL, thereby affording the corresponding DESs having good ability to dissolve AL. For example, it was obvious that the AL solubility increased with the decrease of the L-Carn/5-MeOSA molar ratio as follows: L-Carn:5-MeOSA(2:1) < L-Carn:5-MeOSA(1:1)

In addition, the dissolution behavior of KL in these developed DESs was obviously different from those of AL, DAL and EHL. Except for three DESs, i.e., ChCl:EG(2:1) (Table 2, entry 7), ChCl:OA(2:1) (Table 2, entry 8), and L-Carn:BA(1:2) (Table 2, entry 9), other examined DESs showed unsatisfactory performance on KL dissolution. Surprisingly, a highest solubility of KL (62.0%) was obtained using ChCl:OA(2:1) as the solvent (Table 2, entry 8).

Furthermore, we examined the influence of dissolution temperature (60, 80, and 100 °C) on lignin solubility in seven optimized DESs with relatively good ability to dissolve all the four types of lignin (Fig. 2 and Table S4). Obviously, the solubilities of lignin increased with the rising of dissolution temperature. For all the determined DESs, the solubilities of the four types of lignin at 100 °C was higher than those at 80 °C. As well-accepted, the viscosity of DESs decreased with the increase of temperature, which was beneficial for the molecular interaction between the DESs and the lignin, thereby promoting the dissolution of lignin at higher temperature. In contrast, when the dissolution temperature decreased from 80 to 60 °C, the

solubility of lignin significantly deceased because the greatly increased viscosity of DESs at lower temperature (e.g., 60 °C) was not conducive to the dissolution of lignin. In particular, the melting point of ChCl:BA(1:2) was near 60 °C, and Bet:BA(1:2) and Bet:5-MeOSA(1:1) became solid at 60 °C (Table S1), making them have no ability to dissolve lignin at this temperature. More specifically, ChCl:OA(2:1) could not dissolve DAL at 60 °C although the other three types of lignin (i.e., AL, EHL, and KL) could be efficiently dissolved by ChCl:OA(2:1) at this temperature. This phenomenon may be related with the property of both DAL and ChCl:OA(2:1), which needed additional works to be revealed.

3.4 Effect of lignin structures on lignin dissolution in the developed DESs As shown in Tables S3 and S4, the solubility in the developed DESs varied with the types of lignin, which was probably caused by their different structures. As well-accepted, there were two aspects in the molecular structures of different lignin samples to affect lignin dissolution. ## 3.5 Investigation of reasons on different performances of the developed DESs From the experimental results in Tables 1 and 2, it could be deduced that ChCl was a preferred HBA to prepare efficient DESs for lignin dissolution considering high solubilities of various types of lignin (i.e., AL, DAL, EHL, and KL) in the developed ChCl-based DESs. Meanwhile, the DESs with BA or EG as the HBD generally showed good adaptability on various types of lignin. Originating from the synergistic effect of the examined HBAs and HBDs, ChCl:EG(2:1) provided satisfactory solubilities (> 40%) for all the four types of lignin (Table S3). As well-known, to break the intramolecular hydrogen bonding is essential to make lignin dissolved. Probably, the different performance of the developed DESs on lignin dissolution originated from their different ability to break intramolecular hydrogen bonding in lignin, which correlated with the properties of DESs, i.e., hydrogen-bonding acidity, hydrogen-bonding basicity, polarity, and dissociation degree (pKa) or acidity.

Generally, Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters (α, β, and π*) are employed to evaluate the hydrogen-bonding acidity (α), hydrogen-bonding basicity (β), and polarity (π*) of a solvent. Thus, we determined the Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters of the prepared DESs (Table S6). After correlating

with the solubility of lignin, it was observed that the DESs with higher α values (> 0.95) generally showed higher solubilities of lignin (Fig. 3). For example, ChCl:BA(1:2) and ChCl:OA(2:1) had much higher α values (1.2198, and 1.3534, respectively), and they showed better performance on dissolving all the determined lignin. As well-known, the higher the α values of the solvents are, the stronger ability of donating hydrogen bonding they have. Thereby, the DESs with higher α values had stronger ability to provide hydrogen bonding to lignin, which was beneficial for breaking the intramolecular hydrogen bonding in lignin, thus enhancing the dissolution of lignin. In contrast with the results of α values, no definite correlation was observed between the β value and the lignin solubility. For instance, the solubilities of the four types of lignin were all unsatisfactory in Bet:5-MeOSA(1:1) although it had the highest β value (2.0263). In comparison, the β value of ChCl:OA(2:1) was only -0.1677, but it showed good performance for all the types of lignin (Table S3). These results implied that the β value (hydrogen-bonding basicity) may be not a suitable index to evaluate the ability of DESs to dissolve lignin. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of polarity (described using π* values) on lignin dissolution. When the DESs having larger π* value, the DESs (e.g., ChCl:BA(1:2) and ChCl:OA(2:1)) could efficiently dissolve AL, EHL and KL, indicating that higher polarity was beneficial for dissolving these three types of lignin. Especially, higher polarity could more promote the dissolution of KL. Additionally, the solubilities of DAL in ChCl:BA(1:2) and ChCl:OA(2:1) were lower than those in ChCl:EG(2:1) and ChCl:EG (1:1) with lower π* values. These results could be well explained by the principle of "Like Dissolves Like". Because the abundant sulfonic acid groups in KL significantly increased its polarity, ChCl:OA(2:1) with highest polarity provided the highest solubility of KL (62.0%). In comparison, as described above, the polarity of DAL was lower owing to the less hydroxyl and carboxylic groups in DAL (Table 3), thereby resulting in the relatively higher solubilities of DAL in ChCl:EG(2:1) and ChCl:EG(1:1) than those in ChCl:BA(1:2) and ChCl:OA(2:1) with larger polarity. Based on the results above, we could deduce that both stronger hydrogen-bonding acidity and matched polarity with the dissolved lignin could promote the dissolution of lignin in the developed DESs. ### 3.6 Characterization of the regenerated lignin from the DES solution The dissolved lignin could be easily regenerated from the biomass-derived acidic DESs (using ChCl:EG(1:1) as an example) with water as the anti-solvent, and the recovered lignin was named RAL, RDAL, RKL and REHL, respectively. The regenerated lignin was characterized by 2D HSQC NMR technique to examine the structure change after dissolution and regeneration process, and the results were described in Fig. S3. It was observed that the signal patterns of the native lignin and the corresponding regenerated one were rather similar, suggesting that the basic structure of the lignin did not change after the dissolution and regeneration process. Moreover, the relative abundances (X/100Ar) of different linkages were quantitatively determined by integrating the related signals (Fig. S3). Notably, all the regenerated lignin showed a decrease in the relative abundances of β-O-4 linkages in comparison with the native lignin, implying the cleavage of β-O-4 linkages during the dissolution and regeneration process. For example, the relative abundances of β-O-4 linkages in RKL were declined to 10.6/100Ar from 21.6/100Ar in the native KL. However, the decrease on the relative abundance of C—C bonds was much fewer compared with the decrease on the relative abundance of β-O-4 linkages, suggesting that the ability of the used acidic DES to cleave the C—C bonds was much lower than that of cleaving β-O-4 linkages. It could be deduced that the breakage of β-O-4 linkages was the main reaction during lignin dissolution in acidic DESs, which was a general phenomenon when lignin was dissolved in acidic DESs 11,39.

These results above implied that the developed acidic DESs could be potentially utilized to promote conversion of lignin into value-added chemicals. Besides, in previous reports, acidic DESs had been applied in lignin conversion. For example, Lopes et al. reported that dissolution of lignin in acidic DES favored the formation of lignin oligomers, which could be further convert into syringol, acetosyringone, vanillic and syringic acids 48. Yuan et al. described that phenolic diketones could be obtained from lignin oil after acidic DES dissolution 49. From the current experiments and the previously reported results, the developed acidic DESs could be highly promising for catalytic conversion

## 4 Conclusions In conclusion, several renewable DESs were designed and constructed using biomass-derived chemicals as the HBAs (i.e., ChCl, Bet, and L-Carn) and protonic HBDs (i.e., OA, BA, EG, and 5-MeOSA). These prepared DESs could dissolve different types of lignin, including AL, DAL, EHL, and KL, and the solubility varied with the types of lignin and the DESs. Interestingly, the DESs prepared using ChCl as the HBA showed better performance and adaptability for different types of lignin. More importantly, the ability of the DESs to dissolve lignin correlated well with their hydrogen-bonding acidity and polarity. When a DES having stronger hydrogen-bonding acidity (a value of > 0.95) and appropriate polarity matching with the dissolved lignin, it would possess relatively good performance on lignin dissolution. Besides, it was observed that HBDs (e.g., BA and EG) or DESs with moderate acidity would be preferred to design robust DESs to dissolve lignin. We believe that the developed renewable acidic DESs have great potential in lignin dissolution and lignocellulose pretreatment. Notably, the finding that DESs with a strong hydrogen-bonding acidity, appropriate polarity, and moderate acidity generally have good ability to dissolve lignin is highly helpful to design innovative biomass-based DESs applied in lignocellulose utilization.

Abstract: Lignocellulose utilization has the unique feature of net-zero carbon emissions. Thus, the utilization of lignocellulose as a renewable alternative to fossil-based carbon resources is one of the most promising strategies to achieve "carbon neutrality". Lignin has been recognized as the most abundant aromatic biopolymer on Earth; hence, it could be the most promising alternative to fossil-based aromatics. The efficient dissolution of lignin is crucial for lignin upgrading, which relies on the design of innovative and robust solvents. Herein, we designed several biomass-derived acidic deep eutectic solvents (DESs) using choline chloride, betaine, and L-carnitine as hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs), and four protic compounds as <::transcription of the content : AL DAL EHL KL DES Lignin 80°C Lignin-DES solution AL Solubility (%) ChCl-based Bet-based L-carn-based DES Solubility (%) pKa 5.04 4.19 1.23 2 1.5 1.0 0.5 0.0 EO-based EA-based OA-based DES : figure::> hydrogen bond donors (HBDs), namely, oxalic acid, benzoic acid, ethyl gallate, and 5-methoxysalicylic acid. The designed DESs can dissolve different types of lignin, including alkali lignin (AL), dealkaline lignin (DAL), enzymatic hydrolysis lignin (EHL), and Kraft lignin (KL). Lignin dissolution was found to be affected by the relative contents of three phenylpropanoid monomers in lignin: syringyl (S), guaiacyl (G), and p-hydroxyphenyl (H) units. More S and fewer H units in lignin could result in higher solubility. G-, S-, and H-type structural units were found in EHL, while AL, KL, and DAL had only G-type structural units. Therefore, EHL could be more easily dissolved than AL, KL, and DAL in the most developed DESs. The hydroxyl group content of the four lignin samples had a significant impact on lignin dissolution. AL (1.98 mmol·g⁻¹) and EHL (1.93 mmol·g⁻¹) had much higher contents of phenolic hydroxyl groups than DAL (0.62 mmol·g⁻¹), implying that AL and EHL had higher polarity than DAL. This resulted in different dissolution behaviors in different DESs with varying polarities. However, the sulfonate groups afforded KL with much higher polarity, thus resulting in the special dissolution behavior of KL. It is to be noted that not all cases of dissolving lignin in the developed DESs conformed to the above rules. Therefore, it is necessary to further explore the effect of the properties of the DESs on the dissolution of different lignins. Choline chloride was the preferred HBA to construct DESs with good performance and adaptability to lignin dissolution, whereas suitable acidity enabled benzoic acid and ethyl gallate to be favorable HBDs. Systematic investigation revealed that an efficient DES for lignin dissolution should possess stronger hydrogen-bonding acidity (α > 0.95) and appropriate polarity matching with the dissolved lignin. In addition, the pKa value of the HBD and the acidity of the DESs were also efficient indices for estimating the performance of an acidic DES in dissolving lignin, and the pKa value and acidity could be well correlated with the polarity. Generally, HBDs (e.g., BA and EG in this study) with moderate pKa values can be employed to construct robust DESs to dissolve lignin with satisfactory solubility. In this context, utilization of renewable and abundant-available biomass has gained worldwide interest ³,⁴. As one of the three main components of lignocellulose, lignin has been recognized as the most abundant aromatic biopolymer on earth, thereby affording lignin being the most promising alternative to fossil-based aromatics (i.e., chemicals and materials) ⁵⁻⁷. Especially, the concept of "lignin-first biorefinery" significantly promotes the development of lignin upgrading to produce useful chemicals and functional materials ⁸⁻¹⁰. Generally, dissolution of lignin in an appropriate solvent is unavoidable to realize the goal of effectively utilizing lignin. However, the complex cross-linked three-dimensional structure greatly hinders lignin dissolution ¹¹. To solve this challenging issue relays on designing robust and innovative solvent systems ¹²,¹³. To date, various solvent systems have been developed to dissolve lignin, including aqueous organic solvents 14-17, liquid ammonia 18,19, ionic liquid (IL)-based systems 20-22, and deep eutectic solvents (DESs) 23-25. Of these developed solvents, DESs are an emerging class of functional solvents, and are generally composed by two components, calling as hydrogen-bond donor (HBD) and hydrogen-bond acceptor (HBA), respectively 26-28. In comparison with other solvent systems for lignin dissolution, DESs have some unique features. For example, DESs have lower volatility than organic solvents. Moreover, the process to prepare DESs is much simpler than that of synthesizing ILs, and organic solvents can be completely avoided for constructing DESs 27,29. More importantly, the components in DESs can accept (for HBAs) or donate (for HBDs) hydrogen bonding, endowing DESs the ability to form hydrogen bonding with lignin, which is indispensable for dissolving lignin in a solvent 11,30. These features make DESs be a highly promising class of solvents to dissolve lignin, and some DESs with good ability to dissolve lignin have been successfully developed. Generally, the DESs using protic chemicals (i.e., 物理化学学报 Acta Phys. -Chim. Sin. 2023, 39 (7), 2212043 (3 of 11) alcohols, carboxylic acids, amides, and phenols) as the HBDs showed stronger capability on dissolution of lignin 31-33. However, the properties of lignin varied with the resources of raw lignocellulose and the extraction strategies to obtain lignin, thereby resulting in the unsatisfactory adaptability of the developed DESs on different types of lignin. Additionally, most of the developed DESs often involved fossil-based chemicals. Utilization of biomass-based derivatives to prepare DESs is a highly attractive strategy to achieve a "closed-loop" biorefinery. Recent works revealed that DESs could be directly prepared using biomass-derived chemicals, affording these DESs being biocompatibility and biodegradability. This feature of biomass-derived DESs enabled one-pot biomass processing with good environmental friendliness and cost effectiveness 34-37. Although biomass-derived DESs have been prepared using choline chloride as the HBA and lactic acid or some lignin monomers as the HBDs for lignin dissolution or biomass pretreatment, the DESs prepared completely from renewable resources are still limited, and their capability of dissolving lignin needs to be further improved 23,38,39. In spite of the encouraging achievements of using DESs to dissolve lignin, innovative and robust DESs completely derived from renewable resources are still highly desirable with the goal of making the dissolution processes green to the greatest extent. In another aspect, how to select HBAs and HBDs to construct robust DESs with high solubility of lignin is also an urgent issue to be solved. To date, there still lack reasonable methods or suitable standard to accurately evaluate the capability of one DES on lignin dissolution, resulting in that much time was wasted to select efficient DESs to dissolve lignin. Therefore, exploring a general rule for evaluation of DES's dissolution capability remains a great challenge. With the purpose of developing robust renewable DESs to dissolve lignin and establish a reasonable index to evaluate the ability of acidic DESs to dissolve lignin, herein, we constructed several renewable acidic DESs using biomass-based HBAs and HBDs. In these designed DESs, choline chloride (ChCl), betaine (Bet), and L-carnitine (L-Carn) were selected as the renewable HBAs, while four biomass-based protic compounds (i.e., oxalic acid (OA), benzoic acid (BA), ethyl gallate (EG), and 5-methoxysalicylic acid (5-MeOSA)) were employed as the HBDs. Four different types of lignin, including alkali lignin (AL), dealkaline lignin (DAL), Kraft lignin (KL), and enzymatic hydrolysis lignin (EHL), were selected to investigate the dissolution ability of the developed DESs. In these four types of lignin, AL was mainly derived from alkaline pulping black liquor and had a complex lignin condensation structure linked by C–C and ether bonds, while DAL was achieved from the residue obtained by alkali treatment of lignocellulose and subsequent acidizing separation. KL was usually produced by the reaction between lignin and lye when lignocellulose was cooked by the kraft method. The hydroxyl ions, sulfur ions and sulfhydryl ions in the kraft cooking liquor would effectively promote de-methoxide of lignin to obtain KL with more phenolic hydroxyl groups. EHL was extracted from the enzymatic residue of lignocellulose, which preserved the original structures (phenolic hydroxyl groups, and ether bonds) of the lignin. It was observed that the obtained DESs could dissolve various types of lignin. Notably, all the DESs using ChCl as the HBA possessed good performance on dissolving lignin, while BA and EG were preferred HBDs to generate robust DESs owing to their suitable acidity (based on the pKa and the δP of trimethylphosphine oxide in 31P NMR spectra). These results represented the major finding of this work, which was beneficial for designing robust renewable DESs to dissolve lignin. ## 2 Experimental section ### 2.1 Materials AL was extracted from softwood pulping black liquor, supplied by Shandong Longlive Bio-Technology Co., Ltd. Benzoic acid (BA, 99.5%), ethyl gallate (EG, 98%), and 5-methoxysalicylic acid (5-MeOSA, 97%) were purchased from Energy Chemical (Beijing, China). Meanwhile, the DESs with BA or EG as the HBD generally showed good adaptability on various types of lignin. Originating from the synergistic effect of the examined HBAs and HBDs, ChCl:EG(2:1) provided satisfactory solubilities (> 40%) for all the four types of lignin (Table S3). As well-known, to break the intramolecular hydrogen bonding is essential to make lignin dissolved. Probably, the different performance of the developed DESs on lignin dissolution originated from their different ability to break intramolecular hydrogen bonding in lignin, which correlated with the properties of DESs, i.e., hydrogen-bonding acidity, hydrogen-bonding basicity, polarity, and dissociation degree (pKa) or acidity. Generally, Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters (α, β, and π*) are employed to evaluate the hydrogen-bonding acidity (α), hydrogen-bonding basicity (β), and polarity (π*) of a solvent. Thus, we determined the Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters of the prepared DESs (Table S6). After correlating with the solubility of lignin, it was observed that the DESs with higher α values (> 0.95) generally showed higher solubilities of lignin (Fig. 3). For example, ChCl:BA(1:2) and ChCl:OA(2:1) had much higher α values (1.2198, and 1.3534, respectively), and they showed better performance on dissolving all the determined lignin. As well-known, the higher the α values of the solvents are, the stronger ability of donating hydrogen bonding they have. Thereby, the DESs with higher α values had stronger ability to provide hydrogen bonding to lignin, which was beneficial for breaking the intramolecular hydrogen bonding in lignin, thus enhancing the dissolution of lignin. In contrast with the results of α values, no definite correlation was observed between the β value and the lignin solubility. For instance, the solubilities of the four types of lignin were all unsatisfactory in Bet:5-MeOSA(1:1) although it had the highest β value (2.0263). In comparison, the β value of ChCl:OA(2:1) was only -0.1677, but it showed good performance for all the types of lignin (Table S3). These results implied that the β value (hydrogen-bonding basicity) may be not a suitable index to evaluate the ability of DESs to dissolve lignin. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of polarity (described using π* values) on lignin dissolution. When the DESs having larger π* value, the DESs (e.g., ChCl:BA(1:2) and ChCl:OA(2:1)) could efficiently dissolve AL, EHL and KL, indicating that higher polarity was beneficial for dissolving these three types of lignin. Especially, higher polarity could more promote the dissolution of KL. Additionally, the solubilities of DAL in ChCl:BA(1:2) and ChCl:OA(2:1) were lower than those in ChCl:EG(2:1) and ChCl:EG (1:1) with lower π* values. These results could be well explained by the principle of "Like Dissolves Like". Because the abundant sulfonic acid groups in KL significantly increased its polarity, ChCl:OA(2:1) with highest polarity provided the highest solubility of KL (62.0%). The regenerated lignin was characterized by 2D HSQC NMR technique to examine the structure change after dissolution and regeneration process, and the results were described in Fig. S3. It was observed that the signal patterns of the native lignin and the corresponding regenerated one were rather similar, suggesting that the basic structure of the lignin did not change after the dissolution and regeneration process. Moreover, the relative abundances (X/100Ar) of different linkages were quantitatively determined by integrating the related signals (Fig. S3). Notably, all the regenerated lignin showed a decrease in the relative abundances of β-O-4 linkages in comparison with the native lignin, implying the cleavage of β-O-4 linkages during the dissolution and regeneration process. For example, the relative abundances of β-O-4 linkages in RKL were declined to 10.6/100Ar from 21.6/100Ar in the native KL. However, the decrease on the relative abundance of C—C bonds was much fewer compared with the decrease on the relative abundance of β-O-4 linkages, suggesting that the ability of the used acidic DES to cleave the C—C bonds was much lower than that of cleaving β-O-4 linkages. It could be deduced that the breakage of β-O-4 linkages was the main reaction during lignin dissolution in acidic DESs, which was a general phenomenon when lignin was dissolved in acidic DESs 11,39. These prepared DESs could dissolve different types of lignin, including AL, DAL, EHL, and KL, and the solubility varied with the types of lignin and the DESs. Interestingly, the DESs prepared using ChCl as the HBA showed better performance and adaptability for different types of lignin. More importantly, the ability of the DESs to dissolve lignin correlated well with their hydrogen-bonding acidity and polarity. When a DES having stronger hydrogen-bonding acidity (a value of > 0.95) and appropriate polarity matching with the dissolved lignin, it would possess relatively good performance on lignin dissolution. Besides, it was observed that HBDs (e.g., BA and EG) or DESs with moderate acidity would be preferred to design robust DESs to dissolve lignin. In this context, utilization of renewable and abundant-available biomass has gained worldwide interest ³,⁴. As one of the three main components of lignocellulose, lignin has been recognized as the most abundant aromatic biopolymer on earth, thereby affording lignin being the most promising alternative to fossil-based aromatics (i.e., chemicals and materials) ⁵⁻⁷. Especially, the concept of "lignin-first biorefinery" significantly promotes the development of lignin upgrading to produce useful chemicals and functional materials ⁸⁻¹⁰. Generally, dissolution of lignin in an appropriate solvent is unavoidable to realize the goal of effectively utilizing lignin. However, the complex cross-linked three-dimensional structure greatly hinders lignin dissolution ¹¹. To solve this challenging issue relays on designing robust and innovative solvent systems ¹²,¹³. To date, various solvent systems have been developed to dissolve lignin, including aqueous organic solvents 14-17, liquid ammonia 18,19, ionic liquid (IL)-based systems 20-22, and deep eutectic solvents (DESs) 23-25. Of these developed solvents, DESs are an emerging class of functional solvents, and are generally composed by two components, calling as hydrogen-bond donor (HBD) and hydrogen-bond acceptor (HBA), respectively 26-28. In comparison with other solvent systems for lignin dissolution, DESs have some unique features. For example, DESs have lower volatility than organic solvents. Moreover, the process to prepare DESs is much simpler than that of synthesizing ILs, and organic solvents can be completely avoided for constructing DESs 27,29. More importantly, the components in DESs can accept (for HBAs) or donate (for HBDs) hydrogen bonding, endowing DESs the ability to form hydrogen bonding with lignin, which is indispensable for dissolving lignin in a solvent 11,30. These features make DESs be a highly promising class of solvents to dissolve lignin, and some DESs with good ability to dissolve lignin have been successfully developed. Generally, the DESs using protic chemicals (i.e., 物理化学学报 Acta Phys. -Chim. Sin. 2023, 39 (7), 2212043 (3 of 11) alcohols, carboxylic acids, amides, and phenols) as the HBDs showed stronger capability on dissolution of lignin 31-33. However, the properties of lignin varied with the resources of raw lignocellulose and the extraction strategies to obtain lignin, thereby resulting in the unsatisfactory adaptability of the developed DESs on different types of lignin. Additionally, most of the developed DESs often involved fossil-based chemicals. Utilization of biomass-based derivatives to prepare DESs is a highly attractive strategy to achieve a "closed-loop" biorefinery. Recent works revealed that DESs could be directly prepared using biomass-derived chemicals, affording these DESs being biocompatibility and biodegradability. This feature of biomass-derived DESs enabled one-pot biomass processing with good environmental friendliness and cost effectiveness 34-37. Although biomass-derived DESs have been prepared using choline chloride as the HBA and lactic acid or some lignin monomers as the HBDs for lignin dissolution or biomass pretreatment, the DESs prepared completely from renewable resources are still limited, and their capability of dissolving lignin needs to be further improved 23,38,39. In spite of the encouraging achievements of using DESs to dissolve lignin, innovative and robust DESs completely derived from renewable resources are still highly desirable with the goal of making the dissolution processes green to the greatest extent. In another aspect, how to select HBAs and HBDs to construct robust DESs with high solubility of lignin is also an urgent issue to be solved. To date, there still lack reasonable methods or suitable standard to accurately evaluate the capability of one DES on lignin dissolution, resulting in that much time was wasted to select efficient DESs to dissolve lignin. Therefore, exploring a general rule for evaluation of DES's dissolution capability remains a great challenge. Meanwhile, the DESs with BA or EG as the HBD generally showed good adaptability on various types of lignin. Originating from the synergistic effect of the examined HBAs and HBDs, ChCl:EG(2:1) provided satisfactory solubilities (> 40%) for all the four types of lignin (Table S3). As well-known, to break the intramolecular hydrogen bonding is essential to make lignin dissolved. Probably, the different performance of the developed DESs on lignin dissolution originated from their different ability to break intramolecular hydrogen bonding in lignin, which correlated with the properties of DESs, i.e., hydrogen-bonding acidity, hydrogen-bonding basicity, polarity, and dissociation degree (pKa) or acidity. Generally, Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters (α, β, and π*) are employed to evaluate the hydrogen-bonding acidity (α), hydrogen-bonding basicity (β), and polarity (π*) of a solvent. Thus, we determined the Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters of the prepared DESs (Table S6). After correlating with the solubility of lignin, it was observed that the DESs with higher α values (> 0.95) generally showed higher solubilities of lignin (Fig. 3). For example, ChCl:BA(1:2) and ChCl:OA(2:1) had much higher α values (1.2198, and 1.3534, respectively), and they showed better performance on dissolving all the determined lignin. As well-known, the higher the α values of the solvents are, the stronger ability of donating hydrogen bonding they have. Thereby, the DESs with higher α values had stronger ability to provide hydrogen bonding to lignin, which was beneficial for breaking the intramolecular hydrogen bonding in lignin, thus enhancing the dissolution of lignin. In contrast with the results of α values, no definite correlation was observed between the β value and the lignin solubility. For instance, the solubilities of the four types of lignin were all unsatisfactory in Bet:5-MeOSA(1:1) although it had the highest β value (2.0263). In comparison, the β value of ChCl:OA(2:1) was only -0.1677, but it showed good performance for all the types of lignin (Table S3). These results implied that the β value (hydrogen-bonding basicity) may be not a suitable index to evaluate the ability of DESs to dissolve lignin. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of polarity (described using π* values) on lignin dissolution. When the DESs having larger π* value, the DESs (e.g., ChCl:BA(1:2) and ChCl:OA(2:1)) could efficiently dissolve AL, EHL and KL, indicating that higher polarity was beneficial for dissolving these three types of lignin. Especially, higher polarity could more promote the dissolution of KL. Based on the principle of "Like Dissolves Like", the DES using a HBD with lower pKa value generally showed higher ability to dissolve lignin (e.g., KL) with more and strong polar groups (i.e., hydroxyl, carboxylic, and sulfonic acid groups), while DAL with less polar groups could be well dissolved in the DES using a HBD with higher pKa value. After correlated with the solubility of lignin, it was observed that the difference on the lignin solubility was not significant when the δp values of the DESs were similar. Notably, the DES (ChCl:OA(2:1)) with the highest δp value showed the best performance on dissolution of KL, while the DES (L-Carn:BA(1:1)) with the lowest δp value showed bad ability to dissolve AL, EHL and KL. Nevertheless, L-Carn:BA(1:1) provided a satisfactory solubility of DAL. Generally, the δp values showed a positive correlation with the polarity. Thus, the influence of DES's acidity on lignin solubility showed similar tendency with the effect of DES's polarity, as discussed above. The regenerated lignin was characterized by 2D HSQC NMR technique to examine the structure change after dissolution and regeneration process, and the results were described in Fig. S3. It was observed that the signal patterns of the native lignin and the corresponding regenerated one were rather similar, suggesting that the basic structure of the lignin did not change after the dissolution and regeneration process. Moreover, the relative abundances (X/100Ar) of different linkages were quantitatively determined by integrating the related signals (Fig. S3). Notably, all the regenerated lignin showed a decrease in the relative abundances of β-O-4 linkages in comparison with the native lignin, implying the cleavage of β-O-4 linkages during the dissolution and regeneration process. For example, the relative abundances of β-O-4 linkages in RKL were declined to 10.6/100Ar from 21.6/100Ar in the native KL. However, the decrease on the relative abundance of C—C bonds was much fewer compared with the decrease on the relative abundance of β-O-4 linkages, suggesting that the ability of the used acidic DES to cleave the C—C bonds was much lower than that of cleaving β-O-4 linkages. It could be deduced that the breakage of β-O-4 linkages was the main reaction during lignin dissolution in acidic DESs, which was a general phenomenon when lignin was dissolved in acidic DESs 11,39. These results above implied that the developed acidic DESs could be potentially utilized to promote conversion of lignin into value-added chemicals. We did not investigate this aspect because lignin conversion was beyond the scope of the current work. ## 4 Conclusions In conclusion, several renewable DESs were designed and constructed using biomass-derived chemicals as the HBAs (i.e., ChCl, Bet, and L-Carn) and protonic HBDs (i.e., OA, BA, EG, and 5-MeOSA). These prepared DESs could dissolve different types of lignin, including AL, DAL, EHL, and KL, and the solubility varied with the types of lignin and the DESs. Interestingly, the DESs prepared using ChCl as the HBA showed better performance and adaptability for different types of lignin. More importantly, the ability of the DESs to dissolve lignin correlated well with their hydrogen-bonding acidity and polarity. When a DES having stronger hydrogen-bonding acidity (a value of > 0.95) and appropriate polarity matching with the dissolved lignin, it would possess relatively good performance on lignin dissolution. Besides, it was observed that HBDs (e.g., BA and EG) or DESs with moderate acidity would be preferred to design robust DESs to dissolve lignin. We believe that the developed renewable acidic DESs have great potential in lignin dissolution and lignocellulose pretreatment.
